analysis.one_liner: Ratifies the FTC's authority to run the national do-not-call registry.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: A federal court had challenged the FTC's legal authority to run the national do-not-call registry, the list consumers sign up to stop telemarketing calls. This bill would have settled the question by writing the FTC's authority into law and ratifying the existing registry rule. It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 2003, but the committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households who do not want telemarketing calls; the bill would have removed the legal uncertainty around the do-not-call registry and locked in the FTC rule that blocks unwanted sales calls to people who have signed up.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the FTC is authorized under the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act to compile and implement a national do-not-call registry [S2][S3].
It ratifies the do-not-call registry provision of the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, which took effect March 31, 2003, giving it a firm statutory footing [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, which would lose the ability to call tens of millions of households that placed themselves on the registry, and the businesses that buy their calling services.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a narrow ratification measure, not a consumer-protection overhaul: it validates one FTC rule rather than adding new limits on telemarketing beyond the registry itself [S2][S3].

Because the registry already existed under FTC rulemaking, the bill's practical effect was to lock in that rule as written, including whatever exemptions and enforcement choices the FTC had made in it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and broad: a legal guarantee that the government can keep running a popular list that blocks unwanted sales calls. The cost falls on a single industry whose business model depends on calling people who did not want to be called. The bill contains nothing beyond the registry rule itself, so its scope is narrow, but what it does is clearly pro-consumer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 24, 2003, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Ted Stevens introduced the bill on September 24, 2003, with Senator Hollings, 'to ratify the authority of the Federal Trade Commission to establish a do-not-call registry' [S1][S3].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no committee vote, no Senate floor action, no House action before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
Two senators cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor: one Democrat and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because this bill was a ratification measure, its failure left a gap only briefly: Congress passed companion legislation making the do-not-call registry law that same week, and the registry took effect. So the bill's death changed little for anyone; telemarketers did not gain back access to the registry, and consumers did not lose it. The bill's failure is best read as congressional housekeeping that became unnecessary, not a defeat for consumers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; companion bills made the registry law instead

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ratify the FTC's do-not-call registry authority and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. Fritz Hollings
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction; the text says Stevens introduced it 'for himself and Mr. Hollings.'

for.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye and Sen. George Allen

against.name: Telemarketing industry plaintiffs
against.role: Industry groups suing the FTC in federal court
against.what_they_did: The court challenge to the FTC's legal authority to operate the registry is what created the need for this ratification bill; the committee never acted on it, so no one in the Senate had to oppose it on the record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, his co-introducer a Democrat, and the two cosponsors split one Democrat and one Republican [S4]; no opposing bloc appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill ratifies the do-not-call rule that blocks these firms from calling households that opted out of their market, which is tens of millions of numbers. Their revenue from mass outbound calling would shrink, and their interest in this bill ran directly against the households the bill protected.

industries.industry: Businesses that buy outbound call services
industries.note: These businesses relied on telemarketing as a sales channel and would lose one channel, though the registry also directed sales toward customers who had not opted out.
